article.plain_text:
TL;DR
GPU neoclouds run on airline economics: perishable capacity, 85%+ fixed costs, and returns that live in the last 25 points of utilization.
Wall St financed them with the aircraft playbook: take-or-pay contracts and servers in bankruptcy-remote SPVs at 70% to 80% LTV.
The closer comp is aircraft engine ABS without the maintenance reserve. GPUs burn green time, and there is no shop visit that resets them.
A lot of ink has been spilled in recent days on GPU financing. I wanted to go back to a familiar framework to examine just how this market works. For me, I don't think it's software, the better comp is commercial aviation (specifically aircraft engine ABS). This is going to be a multi part series of blog posts.
Earlier in my career I spent a bunch of years trading ABS, including resi mortgages, solar, credit card loans, student loans, and also aircraft and aircraft securitizations. During my time on Wall St. I bought and sold billions of dollars of structured paper, and then, as an operator (including as Head of Finance at Ramp) structured over $2 billion of asset-backed facilities and other forms of debt financing. Suffice it to say, I did a lot of deals, and many similarities are exceptionally notable.
Over the past two years, private credit has put billions into CoreWeave, Lambda, Crusoe, and a long tail of smaller GPU clouds. I went back to the aircraft framework to see how well it holds up.
A GPU neocloud has basically the same operating model as an airline. Both borrow against their equipment to buy hardware from a concentrated set of manufacturers, park it in scarce physical infrastructure, and rent it out by the hour before the amortization schedule catches up with them.
Here's six specific areas where I think the businesses line up:
 
1. Inventory that expires
An airline sells Available Seat Miles. Once the door closes on a flight, an empty seat is revenue that will never be booked. There is no way to store Tuesday's unsold seat and sell it on Friday.
GPU capacity works the same way. Once an H100 or B200 cluster is energized in a colo, an idle hour can't be sold later, and the debt service accrues whether the rack is busy or not.
2. Fixed costs dominate, marginal costs round to zero
People ask why airlines don't just raise fares enough to stop going bankrupt every decade, and the answer is mostly in the cost structure.
Almost everything about operating a flight is fixed: the lease or EETC payment, crew, gate fees, and the fuel needed to get the airframe to cruising altitude. Those costs are the same with 12 passengers on board or 200. One more passenger costs a few dollars of fuel and a can of soda. Once the flight is on the schedule, a $65 fare beats an empty seat priced at $1,000.
Neoclouds face a similar dynamic:
Fixed costs are an 8x GPU server ($300,000+), a 10-year lease on 60kW+ of liquid-cooled rack space, and 10% to 14% debt service. Together these run well over 85% of the cost base, and an idle cluster still draws meaningful baseline power and cooling.
The marginal cost of taking a GPU from 0% to 100% utilization is just the incremental electricity, roughly $0.05 to $0.07 per kWh, which works out to pennies per GPU-hour.
With a cost base like that, one metric dominates: load factor for an airline, cluster utilization for a neocloud. Airlines generally need load factors around 80% to break even. A debt-financed GPU cluster needs roughly 65% to 75% utilization to cover debt service, hardware amortization, colocation, and power. Below that line the operator is burning equity, and nearly all of the return on invested capital is earned in the band between breakeven and full utilization (basically between 75% and 100% utilization).
3. Squeezed between the OEM and the landlord
Airlines are stuck between the companies that build the planes and the airports that control the gates, and neoclouds have the same problem.
NVIDIA is Boeing and Airbus rolled into one. It captures most of the industry's gross margin at the point of sale and sets a release cadence (Hopper, Blackwell, Rubin) that keeps operators on a permanent CapEx cycle, much like the airframers claw back airline profits through aircraft pricing and engine upgrade cycles whenever carriers start earning excess returns.
On the real estate side, planes are useless without takeoff and landing slots at constrained hubs like Heathrow, JFK, or LaGuardia. In compute, the scarce input has shifted from silicon to powered shells and grid interconnects. Locking up 100+ MW of high-density, liquid-cooled capacity with cheap power and an energized interconnect is the neocloud version of owning slots at a fortress hub.
4. Yield management: three cabins
No operator can afford to fly empty, and not every customer needs the same reliability. Neoclouds have landed on the same cabin segmentation airlines built forty years ago.
First class (multi-year take-or-pay): Frontier labs and hyperscalers sign 3 to 5 year contracts for large, contiguous InfiniBand clusters of 16,000+ GPUs. A $500 million training run can stall on a single bad node or latency spike, so these buyers pay a fixed rate regardless of usage to lock in uptime. This is the cabin the debt facility gets underwritten against.
Economy (on-demand bare metal and VMs): Startups and enterprise teams renting 8 to 64 GPUs by the hour or month for fine-tuning and inference. Switching costs are low, churn is high, and buyers compare hourly rates across aggregators the way leisure travelers sort Google Flights by price.
Standby (spot and batch): 500 idle GPUs at 3am on a Sunday get sold at a 60% to 80% discount, priced just above marginal power. Fault-tolerant work (batch processing, synthetic data generation, academic jobs) fills the gap and gets preempted on 30 seconds' notice when a full-fare customer shows up at the gate.
5. The EETC of silicon
With that much operating overlap, Wall Street brought over aviation's financing playbook too.
For decades, airlines with sub-IG balance sheets have funded their fleets through EETCs and aircraft ABS. The pitch to credit investors is that you are lending against standardized collateral and contracted lease payments held in a bankruptcy-remote SPV, rather than against the airline itself.
Blackstone, Magnetar (I was a founding employee at Crayhill Capital, a former Magnetar spinout), Carlyle and others brought the same structure to GPUs. The neocloud signs a multi-year take-or-pay contract with an IG or well-capitalized counterparty, drops the contract and the NVIDIA servers into a bankruptcy-remote SPV, and borrows at 70% to 80% LTV and 9% to 14% to buy the cluster. Contracted cash flows amortize the debt over 36 to 48 months, and equity is left holding unencumbered hardware at maturity.
6. GPUs are engines, data centers are airframes
I'd push the analogy one step further. A GPU cluster maps better to an aircraft engine than to a whole plane, and the data center (powered shell, cooling loop, grid interconnect) is the airframe.
An airframe is a long-duration shell: a tube with wings, avionics, and a cabin. The engines (CFM56, LEAP, GEnx) do the work, and two of them often account for 40% to 50%+ of a narrow-body's value. Late in an aircraft's life, the engines can be most of what the package is worth while the airframe heads toward part-out.
In a neocloud, the powered shell is the airframe. The building, the 100 MW utility interconnect, the substations, and the liquid-cooling manifolds have a 20 to 30 year economic life, which makes them the long-duration collateral. The GPU is the engine, turning megawatts into tokens, and it comes off the wing every few years while the shell keeps running for decades.
This matters because on the ABS desk, whole-aircraft deals and standalone engine ABS (the Willis Lease and Shannon Engine Support shelves, for example) trade on different credit curves. Three underwriting variables change immediately:
 
Most GPU debt today is sized like whole-aircraft ABS, assuming slow, linear depreciation on a cohesive asset. The collateral behaves like engine ABS with no maintenance reserve.
Anyway, this post is running long. In Part 2 I'll talk about why the Aircraft Engine ABS analogue is so important, and where this analogy breaks down, and also where there are interesting opportunities and where I think smart guys with ABS experience should be building. Stay tuned.
This post also lives on my site, with the tables in full: alexyangsong.com/blog/aluminum-to-silicon. Follow along here for Part 2.

However, as I have said for awhile, I believe $PRME represents a paradigmatic VC-style investment with a long-term upside that dwarfs any other opportunity in biotech history. 

It is far more of a $PLTR or $LLY (or more) in terms of prospective upside, than even an $ALNY or $VRTX or $REGN.

(1) $PRME has the most versatile gene editor, with the demonstrated capability of being able to correct the gene mutations that are the fundamental root cause of monogenic diseases. In fact, it can address 89%+ of the known pathogenic gene variants, if delivery to cells beyond the liver and HSCs can be solved.

(2) Its current primary in-clinic liver targets (AATD, Wilson's Disease) are massive indications in their own right. Success in those alone would justify a valuation north of $10Bn, and we already know that LNPs effectively get gene editors to the liver (see $BEAM).

(3) Successful development of $PRME's primary pre-clinical editor for Cystic Fibrosis (which requires solving delivery to the lungs) would justify a valuation north of $100Bn. $VRTX’s market cap, largely due to Trikafta (CF drug), is evidence of that that. 

(4) $PRME has already delivered a functional cure to two patients with the ultra-rare disease Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD).

(5) Importantly, the FDA has now both cleared the way for $PRME to economically develop therapeutics for ultra-rare diseases like CGD by requiring far less clinical data before approval (removing a key drug development bottleneck), as well as cleared the way for far more rapid approval of editors for different mutations that underlie the same genetic disease (again removing a critical drug development bottleneck). This alone is tremendously unique in the biotechnology space.

A library of editors for ultra-rare disease enabled by this regulatory framework is also a substantial source of revenue in its own right.

(6) Finally, David Liu and his lab at the Broad Institute continues to drive substantial innovation in prime editing. The value of a Nobel Prize level scientific talent leading an ongoing innovation engine for a biotechnology company should not be undersold. The value of this work can be seen in things like the OptiPrime AI they developed to optimize the selection of pegRNAs for a given disease.

______

A lot of biotech investors are scared off of a company like this. A few of the reasons include: 

(i) the devastation CRISPR stocks wreaked on portfolios in earlier days
(ii) a lack of precedent for a biotechnology that addresses the known underlying cause of this many diseases with this level of demonstrated efficacy
(iii) the reality that biotech’s graveyard is riddled with promising and much hyped therapeutics that have failed, and an understandable resultant disdain for grand forward looking projections

However, I do think unless a black swan safety event occurs, $PRME holds fundamentally different prospects than other biotechnologies. 

We have simply never had a biotechnology that can fix the underlying cause of this many serious diseases with a swap of an RNA strand, much less have those diseases be ones for which we KNOW precisely what the underlying cause is (in $PRME's case the genetic mutations underlying genetic diseases) AND for which the therapeutic appears capable to the degree of $PRME's editor of actually fixing that underlying cause (in $PRME’s case efficiently writing in new nucleotides in place of genetic mutations in cells it reaches).

The truth is a lot of the classic biotech frameworks don’t really apply here (so long as a platform level safety event doesn't occur, which is its biggest risk, IP protection probably its second), and even the smartest people struggle with context switching and thinking in the exponential. 

In fact, I would say that often times biotech's and pharma's culture biases against these types of grand visions, because they (rightly) understand biology is really, really hard. Far harder than many people in tech seem to appreciate.

At the same time, most generalist investors don’t know enough to understand why $PRME is different than $CRSP,  $EDIT, $NTLA etc.  To them, it’s just another gene editing company, and haven’t those things done terribly? That's probably true even for people like Paul Graham who have publicly commented on the fact that gene editing will yield enormous companies.

I think therein lies the current opportunity. 

And, it's an opportunity that exists even though a vastly less versatile and capable competitor was bought out by $LLY for 1.0 - $1.3Bn at the worst of the biotech bear market for more than $PRME's current market cap (<$800M). So, aside from a platform level black swan safety event...the downside for $PRME would appear substantially capped over the long-term.

Finally, Anthropic saying it might have found something that looks like CRISPR (read a gene editor) when it was in full IPO pump mode is a key tell. 

Biology is in many ways the Holy Grail for the frontier AI companies, especially Anthropic. They may spew a lot of BS about their capabilities...all human disease is not being cured in the next few years. However, Anthropic IS very good at determining what objective would drive the most value if it were to be achieved. 
A gene editor capable of curing 89% of the genetic variants that underlie genetic disease is precisely that Holy Grail. And, that's even before we start talking about risk factors like APOE4, etc. 

$PRME quite literally ALREADY HAS that editor Anthropic intimated they might someday be able to develop when in full IPO pump mode. 

I have no idea what $PRME’s price does in the short-term. However, I continue to believe it has the potential to transform the face of medicine in unprecedented fashion, and the degree to which it is underpriced is enormous.

我一开始接触神经科学比较晚，大概是2023年的时候。那时在其他人还在感受大一生活的时候，我一心想要创造一个刀剑神域和头号玩家一样的世界，我在知乎发问，跑到国内几乎应该是唯一开设神经科学本科专业的上海纽约大学“求仙问卜”，最后得到的结论是，神经科学，脑科学，电子工程，硬件、软件结合到极致，就算再给人类20年的时间，我也看不到那一天。

当时教授给我的第一个原因是脑。他的理由是人类大脑到今天为止（2023.11我问他的时候），根本没有被彻底建模和理解。这一点不是所谓的脑开发，而是脑机接口做到刀剑神域也就是NerveGear的阶段本质上需要人类科学彻底把脑、意识的问题彻底弄清楚，而如今脑科学领域里，关于大脑的系统论仍然是一盘散沙。

还有就是大众关于侵入式神经科技的认知。侵入式，医疗可用，大众却接受不了芯片入脑（章鱼博士乱入）的不便捷。但如果是非侵入式，解码效率太低，准确性不足。这就是最大的问题之一。

不过，三年过去了，AI发展到今天这个程度，对神经科学、神经科技的发展绝对是有根本性影响的。

现在最大的突破之一，就是连接组学。想想吧，要画出神经元之间的电路图，得在海量电镜切片里追踪每一根神经纤维，以前靠人工几乎不可能完成。AI 自动分割之后，近年来完成了果蝇全脑约 14 万个神经元的连接图，小鼠一立方毫米皮层的图谱也做出来了。
这是在给一盘散沙的系统论补地基。
而且，在各大高校和研究所，用 AI 拟合神经活动，再反过来猜测大脑可能在做什么计算，已经是很活跃的方向。

我可以毫不客气地说，就现在的智能发展速度，脑科学的系统论很有可能不再是一盘散沙。这就好比我们要破解一款超级计算机，以前连电路板上的微米级铜线是怎么连的都不知道，现在AI会直接帮我们把硬件电路图给逆向打印出来。

非侵入式信号效率低、准确性差的问题也可以被AI的高维降噪和模式识别能力暴力破解。
现在的AI，早就不再是死板地去解码某一个特定的脑电波或功能磁共振信号。即使把大脑信号是外星语言。
语义解码器的存在就在于此。
科学家们可以利用类似GPT的架构，让AI去学习人类大脑在思考、听故事、看画面时的脑区激活模式。也就是说，即使非侵入式信号充满了噪音，更强大的AI也能通过强大的上下文预测能力，把这些模糊的信号精准翻译成连续的文本或画面。

神经科学，一定会被AI重塑。我们会通过以脑机接口为主的神经科技看到这一切。
